events.title: Wagner's Ring Cycle Premieres
events.blurb: A 63-year-old German composer presented the first complete four-night performance of a 15-hour operatic cycle he had been writing, off and on, for 26 years, at a festival opera house in a Bavarian town he had specifically had built to host it. Audiences included Tchaikovsky, Liszt, Grieg, Bruckner, the emperor of Germany, and the emperor of Brazil. The complete run was a financial disaster.
events.revealBlurb: August 13-17, 1876 — Richard Wagner at the Bayreuth Festspielhaus, Bayreuth. The festival runs to this day; tickets are difficult to obtain. Wagner's anti-Semitic essays, and the Nazi regime's later embrace of his work, have cast a lasting shadow.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: Sgt. Pepper's Released
events.blurb: A four-person British pop group released an album that redefined popular music's ambitions. Recorded over 129 days, it experimented with orchestral arrangements, studio sound effects, Indian classical instruments, a pig from a farmyard, and a final 42-second tape loop designed to be audible to dogs. The cover showed the band as an imaginary marching band in front of a crowd of cardboard-cutout cultural heroes. It sat at number one on both sides of the Atlantic for months.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1967 (UK) — Sgt. Pepper's Lonely Hearts Club Band by the Beatles. Peter Blake designed the cover; the cardboard figures included Marilyn Monroe, Karl Marx, and Edgar Allan Poe. Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr are the only surviving Beatles today.

events.title: Elvis Presley Dies
events.blurb: A 42-year-old singer was found unresponsive on a bathroom floor of his Memphis mansion in the early afternoon and pronounced dead at a local hospital an hour later. The cause was heart failure, probably exacerbated by a cocktail of barbiturates prescribed by his personal physician. 80,000 mourners lined the four-kilometre route to the cemetery; his face had appeared on 150 magazine covers in his lifetime and would appear on tens of thousands more after his death.
events.revealBlurb: August 16, 1977 — Elvis Presley at Graceland, Memphis. An autopsy found 14 different drugs in his system. His doctor, George Nichopoulos, had his license revoked years later. "Elvis sightings" began the day after the funeral and have never entirely stopped.

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Napster Launched
events.blurb: A 19-year-old Northeastern University student released a peer-to-peer file-sharing program that let any user share their digitized music collection with any other user, anywhere in the world. Within 18 months, 80 million registered users were trading tens of millions of MP3 files a day. The recording industry sued; one rock band's lead drummer famously delivered a list of his fans using the service to Napster's offices in person.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1999 — Shawn Fanning. The suing drummer was Lars Ulrich of Metallica. Napster was shut down by a 2001 court ruling; the brand was later bought, sold, and reused several times, most recently by Algorand.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.

events.title: Snowden Leaks Begin
events.blurb: Two newspapers published articles based on documents leaked by a 29-year-old former NSA contractor, revealing that the U.S. government had been conducting bulk collection of American phone records from a major telecommunications company under a secret court order. The revelations continued for years; the leaker fled to Hong Kong and, after attempting to transit to Ecuador, spent years stranded in the transit zone of a Moscow airport.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 2013 — Edward Snowden, via Glenn Greenwald at The Guardian and Barton Gellman at The Washington Post. Snowden received Russian citizenship in September 2022. Remains wanted on espionage charges in the U.S.

events.title: "Ain't I a Woman?" Speech
events.blurb: A formerly enslaved itinerant preacher, who had walked from slavery in New York state to freedom two decades earlier, rose unexpectedly at a women's rights convention in an Ohio town and delivered a short extemporaneous speech challenging male clergymen who had argued women were too weak and delicate to deserve equal rights. Her rhetorical refrain, reported variously in the surviving transcripts, demanded to know why the same logic did not apply to her, a Black woman who had done every kind of hard labour there was.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1851 — Sojourner Truth at the Akron Women's Rights Convention. The famous phrasing "Ar'n't I a woman?" appeared in a recreation written 12 years later by Frances Dana Gage. Truth's actual speech was reported in 1851 without it.

events.title: 19th Amendment Ratified
events.blurb: Seven decades after a convention in upstate New York had narrowly resolved that women ought to vote, a Tennessee state legislator cast the deciding vote for his state's ratification — after reading a telegram from his mother urging him to do so. Women across the United States gained the national vote in time for the November presidential election, in which 8 million new voters participated.
events.revealBlurb: August 18, 1920 — the deciding vote was cast by Harry T. Burn, age 24. His mother's letter read: "Hurrah, and vote for suffrage. Don't keep them in doubt." The amendment was certified on August 26, now Women's Equality Day.

events.title: Equal Pay Act Signed
events.blurb: A U.S. president signed legislation making it unlawful for employers to pay women less than men for equal work on jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility. The law had been introduced 18 years earlier and passed only after being narrowed so far that it exempted executive, administrative, and professional employees — and explicitly did not cover many of the sex-segregated job categories where the pay gap was worst.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1963 — John F. Kennedy. It amended the Fair Labor Standards Act. The wage gap between full-time working men and women has narrowed from 60 cents on the dollar in 1963 to roughly 82 cents today — not yet zero, and progress stalled for most of the 2010s.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Anita Hill Testifies
events.blurb: A 35-year-old law professor at a large university in the central U.S., subpoenaed by the Senate Judiciary Committee considering a Supreme Court nomination, testified publicly on live television that the nominee — her former supervisor at a federal agency — had sexually harassed her nearly a decade earlier. The all-male Senate committee confirmed him anyway by a 52-48 vote. The hearings galvanized a wave of women candidates; 47 won congressional seats the following year.
events.revealBlurb: October 11-13, 1991 — Hill testified against Clarence Thomas. Thomas was confirmed October 15 and is still on the Court. The 1992 elections were dubbed "the Year of the Woman" — though they still left women only 10 percent of Congress.

events.title: "We Shall Fight" Speech
events.blurb: A prime minister who had been in office barely a month stood in a parliamentary chamber and delivered a report on a catastrophic military retreat, then pivoted to an uncompromising catalogue of every terrain — beaches, landing grounds, fields, streets, hills — across which his country would resist, closing with a flat refusal to ever surrender.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1940 — Churchill's "We Shall Fight on the Beaches" speech to the House of Commons. He reportedly muttered to a colleague immediately after: "And we'll fight them with the butt ends of broken beer bottles because that's bloody well all we've got." The line never made the official record.

events.title: Atlantic Charter
events.blurb: The leader of a neutral superpower and the leader of a beleaguered island nation met secretly aboard warships anchored off a foggy Newfoundland coast and jointly published a declaration of eight principles for the postwar world — including self-determination for peoples, freedom of the seas, and disarmament of aggressor nations — without committing either country to fight.
events.revealBlurb: August 14, 1941 — FDR and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter from HMS Prince of Wales and USS Augusta in Placentia Bay. The US was still technically neutral. The document became the founding framework for the United Nations. Churchill later noted that when the two men sang "O God Our Help in Ages Past" on deck, he felt the war was won.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Operation Torch Landings
events.blurb: American forces entered the ground war for the first time, landing simultaneously at three points along a North African coastline controlled by a French administration that had to decide within hours whether to fight the new arrivals or join them against a common enemy. The simultaneous approach from both directions trapped an entire Axis army between closing forces.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 1942 — the first major American offensive operation of the war in the European theatre. French commanders initially resisted; Vichy French forces fired on US troops and sank a destroyer. A ceasefire was agreed three days later on November 11 — the 24th anniversary of the World War I Armistice.

events.title: D-Day Landings
events.blurb: 156,000 Allied troops crossed the English Channel and landed on five code-named beaches along an 80-kilometre stretch of Normandy coast, supported by 11,000 aircraft sorties and 7,000 naval vessels. A massive deception operation convinced enemy commanders the real target was 300 kilometres further east.
events.revealBlurb: June 6, 1944 — Operation Overlord. Eisenhower carried a note in his pocket taking full blame if it failed. The "Mulberry" artificial harbours, towed across the Channel in pieces, unloaded two million tons of supplies in the months that followed. The first soldier ashore on Sword Beach was a British piper playing "Blue Bonnets Over the Border."

events.title: Marshall Plan Announced
events.blurb: At a Harvard commencement address, a U.S. Secretary of State proposed a massive economic recovery program for a continent devastated by six years of total war. Over four years, $13 billion in aid flowed to 16 western European nations, rebuilding factories, ports, and farms and tying their economies tightly to Washington.
events.revealBlurb: June 5, 1947 — George Marshall took ten minutes. The USSR and its satellites were invited to join; Stalin refused and forbade Poland and Czechoslovakia from participating. Adjusted for inflation, the plan would cost over $150 billion today.

events.title: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg Executed
events.blurb: Julius and Ethel Rosenberg were executed by electric chair at Sing Sing Prison, having been convicted of passing atomic bomb design secrets to the Soviet Union — making them the only American civilians executed for espionage during the Cold War. Their case divided the nation, with their guilt debated in editorial pages, union halls, and diplomatic cables around the world.
events.revealBlurb: June 19, 1953 — Ossining, New York. Ethel Rosenberg required three jolts of electricity before she died; Julius was pronounced dead after the first. Subsequent release of Soviet archives confirmed Julius was a spy; historians still debate the extent of Ethel's involvement.

events.title: Khrushchev Secret Speech
events.blurb: Speaking to a closed session of the Soviet Communist Party's 20th Congress, a new premier delivered a four-hour denunciation of his predecessor's personality cult, show trials, and mass purges. The text was supposed to remain secret but leaked within months, shattering communist movements worldwide and launching a partial cultural thaw at home.
events.revealBlurb: February 25, 1956 — Nikita Khrushchev, three years after Stalin's death. A Polish journalist smuggled the text to Israeli intelligence, who gave it to the CIA. Millions of Soviet prisoners were rehabilitated in the following years.

events.title: SALT I Signed
events.blurb: In the ornate Vladimir Hall of the Kremlin, the leaders of the two superpowers signed the first treaty limiting strategic nuclear weapons. It froze the number of intercontinental and submarine-launched ballistic missiles on each side at then-current levels and restricted anti-missile defenses. Neither arsenal shrank, but the race for ever more warheads finally acquired guardrails.
events.revealBlurb: May 26, 1972 — Nixon and Brezhnev in Moscow. The ABM Treaty signed the same day restricted each side to two (later one) missile defense sites. The US withdrew from it in 2002 under George W. Bush.

events.title: Tiananmen Square Protests
events.blurb: For seven weeks, student demonstrators occupied the vast plaza at the heart of the Chinese capital, demanding democratic reforms, press freedom, and an end to official corruption. Their ranks swelled into the hundreds of thousands. Then the government declared martial law, rolled tanks into the city, and cleared the square overnight, killing hundreds or thousands of civilians in the streets around it.
events.revealBlurb: June 4, 1989 — the crackdown. The iconic image of a lone man stopping a column of tanks was taken on June 5 from a hotel balcony. His identity remains unknown. The topic is still heavily censored inside China.

events.title: Sargon Founds the Akkadian Empire
events.blurb: A royal cupbearer of Mesopotamian origin, whose own infancy legends described a reed-basket journey down a river, overthrew his king and went on to subdue the patchwork of Sumerian city-states that had squabbled for centuries. He united them under a single administration that stretched from the Mediterranean coast to the Persian Gulf, establishing what is generally considered the first empire in human history.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2334 BCE — Sargon of Akkad. His dynasty lasted roughly 180 years before collapsing under external pressure. His granddaughter Enheduanna, high priestess at Ur, became the first named author in world literature. The famous "Mask of Sargon" bronze portrait is either him or a successor — ambiguous.

events.title: Peloponnesian War Begins
events.blurb: Tensions between a democratic maritime empire led by Athens and an aristocratic land-based league led by Sparta erupted into open war when Spartan forces invaded Athenian-allied territory. The war would last 27 years, consume Greek wealth, shatter Athenian power, and undermine Greek confidence in the democratic project. A historian who had commanded an Athenian force early in the war produced a narrative account considered a founding masterpiece of Western historiography.
events.revealBlurb: 431 BCE — Athens vs. Sparta. The historian was Thucydides. A plague in 430 BCE killed perhaps a quarter of the Athenian population, including the city's leader Pericles. Athens finally surrendered in 404 BCE after its fleet was destroyed at Aegospotami; Socrates was executed in Athens five years later.

events.title: Battle of Gaugamela
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's force of 47,000 defeated a Persian imperial army of perhaps 250,000 in the open plains of a Mesopotamian valley. The Macedonian king personally led the decisive cavalry charge at a gap that opened in the Persian centre when its king's bodyguards shifted to counter a feint on the wings. The Persian king fled the field, abandoning his empire; he was murdered by his own satraps a year later. Alexander entered Babylon as the new lord of Asia.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 331 BCE — Alexander III of Macedon vs. Darius III of Persia. Alexander had refused his general Parmenion's advice to attack at night; he reportedly said "I will not steal my victory." Darius fled to Bactria, where he was killed by his cousin Bessus — who was then captured and executed by Alexander.

events.title: Death of Alexander the Great
events.blurb: A Macedonian king who had conquered territory from Greece to northwest India died after a two-week fever in Nebuchadnezzar's palace in Babylon, aged 32. His generals immediately divided his empire into competing successor kingdoms, triggering a half-century of wars called the Wars of the Diadochi.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Secretariat Wins the Triple Crown
events.blurb: A three-year-old chestnut colt won the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in a world-record time of 2 minutes 24 seconds, becoming the first Triple Crown winner in 25 years. His margin of victory and track record remain unmatched; television viewers watching the broadcast described the race as looking like a different event from the others.

events.title: Michael Jordan's Last Shot
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Chicago Bulls star took a jump shot from the top of the key with 5.2 seconds remaining in game 6 of an NBA Finals, giving his team an 87-86 lead over the Utah Jazz in a Salt Lake City arena. Jordan's defender had slipped; the shot rattled home. The Jazz could not tie; the Bulls clinched their sixth championship in eight years. It was the last shot Jordan would take as a Chicago Bull; within weeks the team would break up and he would retire for the second time.
events.revealBlurb: June 14, 1998 — Michael Jordan's "Last Shot" over Bryon Russell. He scored the Bulls' final 8 points of the game. The 1997-98 team was documented in ESPN's 2020 "The Last Dance," which drew enormous audiences during the COVID pandemic lockdown.

events.title: Cubs Win World Series
events.blurb: The Chicago Cubs won their first World Series championship in 108 years, defeating the Cleveland Indians in a 10-inning seventh game interrupted by a rain delay. The Cubs' championship drought — dating back to 1908 — was the longest in American professional sports. Their 1945 loss had been attributed by fans to the "Curse of the Billy Goat," thrown at the owner of a neighbourhood tavern who had been asked to remove his pet goat from a World Series game.
events.revealBlurb: November 2-3, 2016 — Cubs 8, Indians 7 in 10 innings at Progressive Field, Cleveland. The game ended at 12:47 AM local time on November 3. Cubs manager Joe Maddon, third baseman Kris Bryant, and first baseman Anthony Rizzo led the championship team. Chicago celebrated with a victory parade of 5 million people.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: CNN Launches
events.blurb: A 24-hour cable news network began broadcasting from a converted country-club headquarters in a southeastern U.S. city, defying widespread industry skepticism that there was enough daily news to fill a full day of programming. The network's first broadcast began with its founder and his wife standing in front of an American flag. Its approach — continuous live coverage, rolling updates, no fixed broadcast schedule — eventually reshaped how all news was delivered.
events.revealBlurb: June 1, 1980 — Ted Turner's Cable News Network, Atlanta. The Gulf War coverage in 1991, broadcast live from Baghdad as bombs fell, established CNN's dominance. Turner had filmed a doomsday video, intended to play only at the literal end of the world, saying farewell to viewers.

events.title: Ghostbusters Released
events.blurb: A comedy directed by and starring several members of a Saturday Night Live cast followed a team of parapsychology PhDs turned paranormal exterminators in New York City. The film grossed $282 million on a $30 million budget and became the highest-grossing comedy to that point. Its theme song, written under deadline pressure, sat at number one on the Billboard Hot 100 for three weeks. A marshmallow man the size of a skyscraper became the film's most memorable villain.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 1984 — Ivan Reitman directing Bill Murray, Dan Aykroyd, Harold Ramis, and Ernie Hudson. Theme song by Ray Parker Jr. The marshmallow costume, worn by actor William Atherton, weighed 45 kg and caused heat exhaustion.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: South Park Premieres
events.blurb: An animated half-hour adult-comedy series about four foul-mouthed 8-year-old boys in a small Colorado mountain town premiered on the Comedy Central cable network. The deliberately crude cut-paper animation style and its topical-to-the-minute production timeline (each episode was produced in a week rather than the months typical for animation) gave it a reactive speed no other animated show could match. It would remain in production for over 25 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1997 — created by Trey Parker and Matt Stone. Their earlier Christmas short, "The Spirit of Christmas," had circulated as a VHS among Hollywood executives in 1995. The show's 1999 feature film nearly received an NC-17 rating; the MPAA gave it R after the creators submitted it six times.

events.title: Archimedes' Principle of Buoyancy
events.blurb: A Greek mathematician established that an object submerged in fluid is buoyed upward by a force equal to the weight of fluid it displaces — a principle explaining why objects float or sink and allowing the density of irregular objects to be measured precisely. The insight reportedly struck the mathematician while stepping into a bath, causing him to run through the streets in excitement.
events.revealBlurb: c. 250 BCE — the "Eureka" bath story was first told by the Roman writer Vitruvius about 200 years after Archimedes lived, so historians treat it sceptically. What is not disputed is that Archimedes wrote it all down carefully in On Floating Bodies, one of the oldest surviving works of physics. He also calculated an approximation of pi accurate to three decimal places.

events.title: Radium Discovered
events.blurb: After months of processing tonnes of uranium ore residue in a leaky shed, two researchers announced the existence of a second highly radioactive element — far more active per gram than uranium alone. The new element glowed faintly in the dark, making the laboratory notebooks radioactive enough to be hazardous even today. The work established radioactivity as an atomic property rather than a chemical reaction.
events.revealBlurb: December 26, 1898 — Marie and Pierre Curie's notebooks are still too radioactive to handle without protection; researchers must sign a waiver to view them in the French national library. Marie Curie remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics (1903) and Chemistry (1911).

events.title: Photoelectric Effect Explained
events.blurb: A paper explained why shining light on a metal surface ejects electrons only when the light exceeds a threshold frequency — never for very bright low-frequency light — by proposing that light itself travels in discrete energy packets rather than continuous waves. The finding resolved a long-standing paradox and extended the quantum idea from heat radiation to light, fundamentally changing the understanding of what light is.
events.revealBlurb: June 9, 1905 — this was the paper that explicitly won Einstein the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics, not relativity. When the Nobel Committee finally awarded it (sixteen years late), they cited this discovery specifically. Einstein reportedly joked that the committee must have found relativity too controversial.

events.title: Higgs Boson Announced
events.blurb: At a packed seminar, two independent experimental teams working at the world's largest particle accelerator announced the observation of a new particle consistent with the long-predicted Higgs boson — the quantum field excitation that gives other fundamental particles their mass. The discovery completed the standard model of particle physics, confirming a prediction made nearly fifty years earlier.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 2012 — Peter Higgs, who had predicted the boson in 1964, was in the audience and reportedly wept. The two experiments — ATLAS and CMS — had been run in blind competition to avoid bias. Higgs and François Englert shared the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year.

events.title: Gravitational Waves Detected
events.blurb: Two massive laser interferometers simultaneously detected a brief chirp of spacetime distortion that lasted a fraction of a second — the gravitational ripple produced by two black holes colliding 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal exactly matched the prediction of general relativity and confirmed that spacetime itself can vibrate, opening a new branch of observational astronomy.
events.revealBlurb: Detected September 14, 2015; announced February 11, 2016 — the team waited five months to check for errors. The signal lasted 0.2 seconds. One scientist described hearing the chirp played as audio as "nature singing to us." Three founders of LIGO — Weiss, Barish, and Thorne — shared the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics.

events.title: The Birth of a Nation Premieres
events.blurb: An American director released a three-hour silent film about a Southern family during the Civil War and Reconstruction, pioneering cinematic techniques that remain standard: close-ups, cross-cutting, battle-scene camera movement. The film portrayed the Ku Klux Klan as heroic and Black people (played mostly by white actors in blackface) as subhuman. Its release coincided with a revival of the real Klan, which had been inactive for 40 years.
events.revealBlurb: February 8, 1915 — D.W. Griffith at Clune's Auditorium, Los Angeles. President Woodrow Wilson hosted a White House screening, calling it "history written with lightning." The NAACP's protest against it was the organization's first major campaign.

events.title: Rashomon Released
events.blurb: A 40-year-old Japanese director released a 88-minute film in which the same violent encounter is recounted by four different participants, none of whom agrees with any of the others. The Venice Film Festival awarded it the Golden Lion the following year, and the world film industry discovered Japanese cinema as a major force. The very title became an English noun: "the Rashomon effect" is the concept of contradictory memories.
events.revealBlurb: August 26, 1950 — Akira Kurosawa. The producers were reportedly baffled by the script and wanted it re-edited. Its Venice win completely blindsided Japanese critics, who had not thought much of the film. It led directly to the global reception of Ozu, Mizoguchi, and Kurosawa's later work.

events.title: The Seventh Seal Released
events.blurb: A Swedish director released a 96-minute black-and-white film about a disillusioned medieval knight, returning from the Crusades to find his homeland ravaged by plague, who plays an extended chess match with a personification of Death to postpone his own. The film's signature image — the knight and Death on a beach chessboard — entered the pantheon of instantly recognizable cinema shots, as did its bleak allegorical mode.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 1957 — Ingmar Bergman, with Max von Sydow as the knight. The chess game has been parodied by Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey, the Muppets, and South Park, among dozens of others. Bergman wrote the screenplay in two weeks.

events.title: Psycho Released
events.blurb: A British-American director released a black-and-white thriller for a third of his usual budget, using his television crew, that broke every Hollywood rule: its marketed star was killed in the shower 45 minutes in, the real story shifted to a different protagonist, and theatrical exhibitors were barred from letting latecomers enter. The 45-second shower sequence, involving 77 camera setups in a week of filming, became the most analyzed passage in thriller cinema.
events.revealBlurb: June 16, 1960 — Alfred Hitchcock, starring Janet Leigh and Anthony Perkins. Hitchcock personally bought up copies of the Robert Bloch novel to limit spoilers. The shower-stabbing sound was a knife thrust into a casaba melon.

events.title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial Released
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American director released a 115-minute family film about a stranded alien befriended by a suburban boy who helps him contact his home planet. The director had developed the story as a way of processing his parents' divorce and his imaginary childhood companion. The film topped the box office for 16 weeks, displaced Star Wars as the highest-grossing film of all time, and moved children to tears for decades.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1982 — Steven Spielberg. Composer John Williams won the Oscar for his score; Spielberg himself didn't. The flying-bicycle silhouette against the moon became the logo of Amblin Entertainment, his production company.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: Fellini's 8½ Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a semi-autobiographical film about a filmmaker suffering a creative block while preparing his next picture, in which the director's own memories, dreams, and erotic fantasies dissolve into the plot he is trying to construct. The Italian title referred literally to the number of films the director had made. It won two Oscars and became the classic film-about-film-making, endlessly quoted by later directors similarly stuck.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 1963 — Federico Fellini, with Marcello Mastroianni as his alter ego. Fellini had genuinely been blocked after a string of successes; the film emerged from trying to work out why. It was remade as a Broadway musical ("Nine") in 1982.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: Toy Story Released
events.blurb: A California animation studio released the first feature film produced entirely with computer-generated imagery, a 81-minute buddy comedy about a child's cowboy doll who feels threatened by a new space-ranger action figure. The studio had spent four years on the film, through three near-cancellations and total rewrites; the resulting picture grossed $390 million and established a new production studio as the dominant force in animation for the next two decades.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1995 — Pixar Animation Studios, directed by John Lasseter. Tom Hanks and Tim Allen voiced Woody and Buzz Lightyear. Pixar had been Apple founder Steve Jobs's expensive side-project; Disney bought them for $7.4 billion in 2006.

events.title: Medgar Evers Assassinated
events.blurb: The NAACP's field secretary in a Southern state was shot in the back in his own driveway as he returned home at 12:30 AM from a meeting, carrying T-shirts that read "Jim Crow Must Go." He died in front of his wife and three children. His killer, a Ku Klux Klan member, was tried twice; both trials ended in hung juries with all-white panels. He walked free for 31 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1963 — Jackson, Mississippi. His killer, Byron De La Beckwith, was finally convicted in 1994 after new witnesses came forward. Medgar's widow Myrlie Evers-Williams spent decades pursuing the case; she later chaired the NAACP.

events.title: March on Washington
events.blurb: A quarter-million Americans — three-quarters Black, a quarter white — gathered between the Washington and Lincoln Memorials on the 100th anniversary summer of the Emancipation Proclamation to demand the passage of civil-rights legislation then stalled in Congress. The event's closing address, given on the steps of the Lincoln Memorial, contained a phrase repeated in eight paragraphs: "I have a dream."
events.revealBlurb: August 28, 1963. MLK's prepared text did not contain "I have a dream" — Mahalia Jackson, behind him on the dais, shouted "Tell them about the dream, Martin!" and he ad-libbed the most famous passage. The Justice Department had 4,000 troops on standby in case of violence. None was needed.

events.title: Loving v. Virginia
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously struck down the laws of sixteen states prohibiting interracial marriage, after a Virginia couple — a white construction worker and his Black and Native American wife — had been awakened in their bed, arrested, and sentenced to a year in jail for being married. The Court called the bans "measures designed to maintain White Supremacy."
events.revealBlurb: June 12, 1967 — Richard and Mildred Loving. They had been legally married in Washington D.C. and returned home to Virginia. Their surname's poetic appropriateness is real, not invented. June 12 is now informally "Loving Day."

events.title: Thurgood Marshall Confirmed
events.blurb: The U.S. Senate confirmed the first African-American justice of the Supreme Court by a vote of 69-11 after a contentious hearing in which Southern senators grilled him on obscure constitutional questions in an effort to embarrass him. He had already argued 32 cases before the Court — and won 29 — as the NAACP's lead attorney. He served 24 years.
events.revealBlurb: August 30, 1967 — confirmed to replace Tom Clark. Lyndon Johnson had said bluntly on tape: "I want folks to look up and see a Negro lawyer up there." Marshall was the grandson of a slave and had been rejected by the University of Maryland law school on racial grounds.

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.

events.title: Battle of Bunker Hill
events.blurb: American militia who had occupied two hills on a peninsula north of Boston overnight were assaulted by British regulars advancing uphill in three waves. The defenders — reportedly told "don't fire until you see the whites of their eyes" to conserve ammunition — inflicted heavy casualties on the first two waves before running out of powder and being driven from the ground. The British held the field but lost over 1,000 men; the American cause gained enormous moral prestige.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1775 — fought mostly on Breed's Hill; misnamed after the adjacent Bunker Hill. British commander: General Thomas Gage. American commander killed in the retreat: General Joseph Warren. Within days, Congress appointed George Washington commander-in-chief.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Battle of Waterloo
events.blurb: A French emperor's army of 73,000 men, attempting to defeat the main Anglo-Allied and Prussian armies separately before they could unite, fought the Anglo-Allied force on a Belgian ridge for most of a muddy Sunday. The Prussian army arrived in the late afternoon on the emperor's right flank; by nightfall the French line had collapsed. The emperor fled; he surrendered to the British at a port three weeks later and was exiled to a rocky island in the South Atlantic.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1815 — Napoleon Bonaparte vs. the Duke of Wellington and Gebhard von Blücher. Napoleon was exiled to Saint Helena and died there May 5, 1821. "Meet your Waterloo" — a decisive and final defeat — entered English as a phrase.

events.title: Battle of Boyacá
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Venezuelan-born general leading a small multinational patriot army of 2,500 men across the Colombian highlands caught a Spanish royalist force in poor defensive terrain and defeated it in a two-hour battle that cost only 13 patriot dead but broke Spanish military power in the region. Within three days the general's army marched into the Colombian capital. The Battle of Boyacá is generally regarded as the decisive engagement of South American independence from Spain.
events.revealBlurb: August 7, 1819 — Simón Bolívar and Francisco de Paula Santander at the Boyacá River, Colombia. Bolívar would go on to liberate Venezuela, Ecuador, Peru, and Bolivia — the last of which was renamed in his honour.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: Raphael's School of Athens
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Umbrian painter completed the second of four monumental frescoes on the walls of the pope's private library at the Vatican, gathering the giants of classical philosophy into a single imaginary architectural space. Plato and Aristotle walk forward from a vanishing point; Pythagoras writes in a book, Euclid draws on a slate, Heraclitus leans alone on a block. The face of Euclid is the architect Bramante; Heraclitus is Michelangelo, working bitterly next door.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Raphael Sanzio, in the Stanza della Segnatura. The rivalry with Michelangelo, then painting the Sistine Ceiling a short walk away, was real; Raphael added him as an afterthought in a late revision.

events.title: Van Gogh Paints The Starry Night
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Dutch painter, voluntarily committed to a mental asylum in a Provençal town, painted from memory — and through the bars of his east-facing window — a night sky filled with swirling nebulae and stars dozens of times their actual size, above a village with an exaggeratedly prominent church steeple. He considered the painting a failure. It is now among the most recognized images in Western art.
events.revealBlurb: June 1889 — Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum, Saint-Rémy-de-Provence. The village in the picture does not match the actual view. The Museum of Modern Art in New York has owned it since 1941. Recent research suggests the sky's swirls resemble actual fluid turbulence.

events.title: Dalí's Persistence of Memory
events.blurb: A 27-year-old Spanish surrealist painted a small oil on canvas — only 24 by 33 cm — showing four pocket watches, one covered in ants, draped limply over a tree branch, a bier, and a distorted horse-headed figure in a landscape of Catalan coast. He said the idea came from contemplating a runny camembert cheese. The ants, the soft watches, and the empty landscape have become visual shorthand for dreamlike unreality.
events.revealBlurb: 1931 — Salvador Dalí. Now in the Museum of Modern Art in New York. Dalí painted a second version, "The Disintegration of the Persistence of Memory," 23 years later. He is said to have visualized in reverse: imagining the picture whole and then painting what he saw.

events.title: Kahlo's The Two Fridas
events.blurb: A 32-year-old Mexican painter produced her largest painting — two life-sized self-portraits seated side-by-side on a bench, their hearts exposed and linked by an artery, against a stormy sky. The double figure depicted her divided heritage (her Mexican and European sides) and also the raw aftermath of her divorce from a fellow painter, which had become final three months earlier. She would remarry him a year later.
events.revealBlurb: 1939 — Frida Kahlo, shortly after divorcing Diego Rivera. Now in Mexico City's Museo de Arte Moderno. It was the largest canvas she ever painted, about 1.7 metres square. Kahlo's work reached superstar popularity only decades after her 1954 death.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Sack of Lindisfarne
events.blurb: A band of Scandinavian raiders beached their longships on the tidal island home of an isolated monastery off the northeast coast of England, slaughtered the monks, and plundered the gold and silver from the gilded shrines. The attack shocked Christian Europe, which had not imagined its remote religious outposts were vulnerable. It marks the conventional beginning of the Viking Age.
events.revealBlurb: June 8, 793 — the monks had left their community undefended on the assumption that the sea was a barrier rather than a road. Alcuin, one of Charlemagne's advisers, wrote: "Never before has such terror appeared in Britain as we have suffered from this pagan race."

events.title: Council of Clermont
events.blurb: The pope, addressing a crowd of French clergy and nobles in an open field outside a central French city after a church council, called on Christendom to take up arms and march east to recover a holy land from Muslim rule. "Deus vult," the crowd cried back — "God wills it." Within three years, 100,000 pilgrims and knights would be on the road.
events.revealBlurb: November 27, 1095 — Pope Urban II. His stated goals shifted in each retelling; the Byzantine emperor had only asked for mercenaries. The First Crusade's armies would surprise everyone, including themselves, by actually reaching Jerusalem.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Battles of Lexington and Concord
events.blurb: That spring morning, British regulars marching to seize a colonial weapons cache at Concord, Massachusetts, exchanged fire with local militia at Lexington before the colonists scattered; at Concord's North Bridge, a second volley triggered a running battle that chased the redcoats back to Boston. The day produced roughly 300 total casualties and the phrase "the shot heard round the world."
events.revealBlurb: April 19, 1775 — Lexington and Concord, Massachusetts. Nobody knows who fired first at Lexington — colonial accounts and British accounts flatly contradict each other. The phrase "shot heard round the world" was written by Ralph Waldo Emerson in 1837, over 60 years after the fact.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Ratified
events.blurb: New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify the proposed Constitution, providing the three-fourths supermajority required to bring the new framework of government into effect and replace the faltering Articles of Confederation. The document created a federal republic with three separated branches of power — a design that had no exact precedent in world history.
events.revealBlurb: June 21, 1788 — New Hampshire. Rhode Island didn't ratify until May 1790 — over a year after the government had already begun operating. North Carolina waited until November 1789, after the First Congress had already convened.

events.title: Marbury v. Madison: Judicial Review Established
events.blurb: Chief Justice John Marshall wrote the unanimous Supreme Court opinion in a case about a disputed judicial appointment, using it to announce that federal courts possessed the power to strike down laws they found incompatible with the Constitution — a power the Constitution itself does not explicitly mention. The ruling transformed the Supreme Court from the weakest branch of government into an equal arbiter of constitutional meaning.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1803 — Washington, D.C. Marshall's genius was ruling against Marbury (who wanted his commission) so Jefferson couldn't refuse to comply, while simultaneously claiming the Court's enormous new power. Jefferson privately hated the decision but was trapped. The ruling wasn't used to strike down another law for 54 more years.

events.title: Taft-Hartley Act Becomes Law
events.blurb: The Republican-controlled 80th Congress overrode President Harry Truman's veto, enacting the Labor-Management Relations Act — known as Taft-Hartley — which restricted union activities, banned secondary boycotts and solidarity strikes, permitted states to pass right-to-work laws, and required union officers to swear they were not Communists. The law fundamentally reshaped the relationship between organized labor and the federal government.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1947 — Washington, D.C. Truman called it a "slave labor bill" in his veto message, though he later used its provisions himself to break the 1952 steel strike. Union membership peaked at about 35% of the workforce in the late 1940s; by 2024 it had fallen to roughly 10%.

events.title: Watergate Break-In
events.blurb: At 2:30 in the morning, Washington D.C. police arrested five men inside the headquarters of the Democratic National Committee at the Watergate complex, where they had broken in to photograph documents and plant surveillance devices. The burglars were connected to the Committee to Re-Elect the President, and the discovery of the break-in and the subsequent cover-up by the Nixon White House eventually destroyed his presidency.
events.revealBlurb: June 17, 1972 — Watergate complex, Washington, D.C. The burglars were caught because a security guard noticed tape on a door latch and called the police. Nixon won re-election in November 1972 in one of the largest landslides in American history — 520 to 17 electoral votes — while the cover-up was already underway.

events.title: Great Wall of China Begun
events.blurb: The first emperor of a unified Chinese state, having conquered the six rival warring kingdoms, ordered existing regional defensive walls in the north linked into a continuous frontier fortification against nomadic incursions. A conscripted army of 300,000 labourers worked for years; many died on the project and were, according to tradition, buried in its foundations. The Ming-dynasty wall, which is what most modern visitors see, was rebuilt over a millennium later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 220 BCE — Qin Shi Huang. The visible stone-and-brick wall is largely Ming-dynasty (1368-1644), built with much better materials. The Qin wall was mostly earthen and only fragments survive. Total length, across all versions, has been measured at 21,196 km.

events.title: Colosseum Inaugurated
events.blurb: A Roman emperor inaugurated a 50,000-capacity elliptical amphitheatre in the capital with 100 consecutive days of gladiatorial games, executions, and staged hunts that killed 9,000 animals. The structure was four stories tall, constructed in travertine and concrete, with a retractable canvas awning (velarium) to shade the spectators. Its name comes from the colossal statue of an earlier emperor that stood nearby. Three quarters of the building still stands today.
events.revealBlurb: 80 CE — inaugurated by Emperor Titus, son of Vespasian who had started construction eight years earlier. The colossal statue in question was of Nero, which Vespasian had rededicated as the sun god. Most of the travertine facing was stripped in medieval times for Renaissance building projects.

events.title: Machu Picchu Built
events.blurb: An Inca emperor's royal estate was built at 2,430 metres on a narrow mountain ridge above a river in the Andes, with 200 stone buildings — agricultural terraces, palaces, temples — arranged on a mountain site that seemed intended for dramatic rather than practical reasons. It was abandoned roughly a century later for unclear reasons, possibly connected to the Spanish conquest of the Inca. The site remained unknown to the Spanish and, largely, to the outside world until 1911.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1450 — emperor Pachacuti. The American explorer Hiram Bingham encountered it on July 24, 1911. Local farmers had never really forgotten it; the "rediscovery" was primarily for outside audiences. It is now one of the New Seven Wonders of the World.

events.title: Hoover Dam Completed
events.blurb: A 221-metre concrete arch-gravity dam across the Colorado River at a deep canyon on the Arizona-Nevada border was completed two years ahead of schedule, creating what was at the time the largest reservoir on the planet. The dam's construction employed 16,000 workers during the worst years of the Great Depression; 96 died during the 5-year project. It generated 2,080 megawatts, ran every light in Las Vegas, irrigated a million acres, and made the Los Angeles basin's growth possible.
events.revealBlurb: September 30, 1935 — originally called the Boulder Dam under Roosevelt's administration; renamed 1947 after Herbert Hoover, who had championed the project as Commerce Secretary. Around 6 million tons of concrete went into it — enough, with less, to pave a two-lane road from San Francisco to New York.

events.title: Channel Tunnel Opens
events.blurb: A 50-kilometre twin-bore railway tunnel under the English Channel opened, linking France to Britain below the sea floor for the first time in 8,000 years. The tunnel had been proposed repeatedly since the early 19th century but had always been shelved on defensive grounds; the end of the Cold War and European integration finally made it buildable. Construction had involved eleven tunnel-boring machines drilling simultaneously from both sides; the breakthrough was within 35 centimetres alignment.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1994 — Queen Elizabeth II and President François Mitterrand cut a ribbon jointly. Total project cost: £9 billion, roughly 80 percent over budget. The tunnel is used by Eurostar passenger trains and the freight-carrying Shuttle. Trains reach 160 km/h underground.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Erasmus Publishes Praise of Folly
events.blurb: A 44-year-old Dutch humanist scholar, passing a week at the London home of his friend Thomas More, dashed off a satirical essay in Latin in which a personified Folly delivered a self-congratulatory oration cataloguing the foolishnesses of every social station — pedantic scholars, superstitious monks, greedy merchants, bloody princes. The essay circulated across Europe in pirated editions within months; it would be read as a scathing critique of the corrupt Catholic Church.
events.revealBlurb: 1511 — Desiderius Erasmus. The pun of the title is trilingual: "Moriae Encomium" in Latin, pointing at Thomas More (Morus) as well as at folly. It was placed on the Papal Index of Prohibited Books in 1559. More, who thought the essay funny, was canonized after being beheaded by Henry VIII.

events.title: Globe Theatre Opens
events.blurb: A London acting company, evicted from their original playhouse when their landlord refused to renew the lease, dismantled the building overnight, carried the timbers across the frozen Thames, and rebuilt them into a new circular theatre on the south bank. Their principal playwright and shareholder produced several of his greatest plays on its stage over the next 14 years, until a cannon effect during a performance of Henry VIII set the thatched roof alight.
events.revealBlurb: 1599 — the Lord Chamberlain's Men; William Shakespeare was a shareholder. It burned on June 29, 1613; was rebuilt; was demolished in 1644 under Puritan hostility to theatre. A faithful replica opened in 1997 near the original site.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: King James Bible Published
events.blurb: An English translation committee of 47 scholars, working in six sub-committees across three cathedrals, completed a new authorized English Bible commissioned seven years earlier by the English king at a church conference. Rather than abandon earlier translations, they drew liberally on William Tyndale's sixteenth-century Protestant version. The resulting text shaped English-language literary style so pervasively that its phrases are still in routine use four centuries later.
events.revealBlurb: 1611 — commissioned at the Hampton Court Conference, 1604. James I of England (and VI of Scotland) authorized it. Its prose cadences, largely inherited from Tyndale, influenced Shakespeare, Milton, Blake, Dickens, and Lincoln. Its Old Testament translation was done primarily at Westminster and Cambridge; the New at Oxford.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: Paradise Lost Published
events.blurb: A blind 58-year-old English poet, dictating to a rotating cast of scribes, completed a 10-book (later 12-book) epic poem retelling the Biblical account of the fall of man from the perspective of a sympathetically characterized Satan. Having narrowly escaped execution for his political writings under the restored monarchy, he was paid ten pounds for the manuscript. It would become the template for English epic poetry.
events.revealBlurb: 1667 — John Milton. He had gone blind in 1652 from untreated glaucoma. His daughters had to be taught to read — including Hebrew, Greek, and Latin — just so they could transcribe his dictations. "The mind is its own place..." is from Book I.

events.title: Walden Published
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Massachusetts essayist, graduate of Harvard, former schoolteacher, and occasional pencil-factory worker, published an account of two years and two months he had spent living in a cabin he had built himself beside a glacier-pond near Concord. The book mixed natural observation, economic criticism, and philosophical reflection. It sold slowly; its reputation grew after the author's early death seven years later, and he is now considered one of the founders of American nature writing.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1854 — Henry David Thoreau. He had lived at Walden Pond 1845-47. The pond was, contrary to legend, a short walk from his family home; his mother did his laundry. Thoreau's civil-disobedience essay would later inspire Gandhi and Martin Luther King Jr.

events.title: Anne Frank's Diary Published
events.blurb: Two years after the liberation of Nazi concentration camps and the death of his teenage daughter in one of them, a Dutch businessman published, after several rejections, an edited version of the diary she had kept during the two years her family had spent hiding in a secret annex behind his Amsterdam office. The book was a modest Dutch bestseller; translated into over 70 languages, it became the most widely read personal account of the Holocaust.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1947 — Otto Frank published "Het Achterhuis" ("The Secret Annex"). Anne had died of typhus in Bergen-Belsen in February 1945, two months before liberation. The diary has sold over 30 million copies.

events.title: Harry Potter First Book Published
events.blurb: A 32-year-old single mother who had drafted most of the manuscript in Edinburgh cafés over six years, on single-parent benefits, published her first novel after twelve rejections from other publishers. The first print run was 500 copies; 300 went to libraries. Children started reading, telling friends, and returning. Within four years the series had become the most successful in publishing history; she would become the first novelist to reach a billion-dollar net worth.
events.revealBlurb: June 26, 1997 — J.K. Rowling, "Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone" (US title: "Sorcerer's Stone"). Her publisher Bloomsbury suggested using "J.K." instead of Joanne because boys might not read a book by a woman. The series has sold over 600 million copies.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Casablanca Premieres
events.blurb: A wartime romance set in a Moroccan cafe — produced on a tight schedule with an often-improvised script — premiered at a New York theater two weeks after Allied troops actually landed in the real-life city, a coincidence that boosted interest. The film's lead actor and actress had expected it to be a forgettable assignment; its dialogue's half-dozen phrases would be quoted by a century of audiences. Neither of the two stars was anyone's first choice for their parts.
events.revealBlurb: November 26, 1942 — Hollywood Theatre, NYC. Director Michael Curtiz, stars Humphrey Bogart and Ingrid Bergman. "Here's looking at you, kid" was Bogart's improvisation. "Play it again, Sam" is never actually said in the film.

events.title: Tokyo Story Released
events.blurb: A Japanese director released a 136-minute film about an elderly provincial couple who travel to the capital to visit their adult children, only to find them too busy with their own lives. Its stationary low-angle camera, dialogues shot face-on toward the audience, and refusal of conventional emotional climax embodied the director's signature style. Polls of international critics and filmmakers regularly rank it among the greatest films ever made.
events.revealBlurb: November 3, 1953 — Yasujirō Ozu. He developed the "tatami-level" camera position — 30 cm off the ground, corresponding to the height of a person seated on a tatami mat. It did not gain a Western reputation until the 1970s; Ozu had died in 1963, never having lived to see his international recognition.

events.title: Jaws Released
events.blurb: A 28-year-old director released a 124-minute thriller about a great white shark terrorizing a New England beach resort. Principal photography, supposed to last 55 days, ran 159; the mechanical shark broke down constantly and was rarely shown, producing the film's signature off-screen menace. Released across a record number of screens nationwide with a saturation TV ad campaign, it invented the summer blockbuster.
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1975 — Steven Spielberg. The shark's malfunctions forced Spielberg to rely on John Williams' two-note score to telegraph the threat. The film caused a measurable drop in US beach attendance for years afterward.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.

events.title: Stonehenge Completed
events.blurb: Over the course of a millennium, Neolithic builders on a chalk plain in southern England erected a circular arrangement of massive standing stones — some weighing 25 tonnes, dragged from quarries over 250 kilometres away — fitted together with mortise-and-tenon joints as if they were timber. The monument aligns with the midsummer sunrise and midwinter sunset. Its precise purpose — ritual, astronomical, funerary — has been debated for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2000 BCE — main sarsen-circle completion on Salisbury Plain. The smaller "bluestones," of volcanic rock, came from the Preseli Hills in Wales. Construction had begun about 5,000 years ago in earthen-bank form. The monument predates the druids by 2,000 years, despite the misattribution.

events.title: Pantheon of Rome Completed
events.blurb: A Roman emperor completed a rebuilt temple, topped with an unreinforced concrete dome 43.3 metres in diameter — the largest dome in the world for over 1,300 years, and still the largest unreinforced-concrete dome ever built. A 9-metre oculus at its apex is the only source of natural light. The dome's concrete mix grew lighter toward the top (using pumice aggregate), and its coffered interior thinned as it rose, reducing weight where it mattered.
events.revealBlurb: c. 126 CE — Emperor Hadrian, rebuilding an earlier Agrippa temple destroyed by fire. It became a Catholic church in 609 CE, which is why it survived intact unlike other Roman temples. Raphael and the Italian kings Victor Emmanuel II and Umberto I are buried inside.

events.title: Taj Mahal Completed
events.blurb: A Mughal emperor completed, 22 years after his beloved queen's death in childbirth, a white-marble mausoleum for her on the bank of a river in a North Indian city. Some 20,000 craftsmen worked on the main structure alone; the dome rises 73 metres, inlaid with semiprecious stones in floral and calligraphic patterns. A matching mosque flanks one side of the tomb; a guest house mirrors it on the other. The emperor's own body joined hers in the crypt in 1666.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1648 — Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal, who died in 1631. The architectural team was led by Ustad Ahmad Lahori. An apocryphal legend claims Shah Jahan cut off the master builders' hands; there is no historical evidence for it. The monument changes colour subtly throughout the day.

events.title: St. Paul's Cathedral Completed
events.blurb: After 35 years of construction replacing a medieval cathedral destroyed in the Great Fire of London, a 68-year-old English architect watched his son install the final piece of his new cathedral's lantern atop its dome — the first cathedral anywhere in the world to have been entirely designed, built, and completed by a single architect within his own lifetime. The triple-domed design, inspired by St. Peter's in Rome, rose 111 metres above the City of London.
events.revealBlurb: 1710 — Sir Christopher Wren. He also designed 52 other London churches after the Great Fire of 1666. He was buried in the cathedral's crypt when he died in 1723 at 90; his memorial reads "Si monumentum requiris, circumspice" — if you seek his monument, look around you.

events.title: Suez Canal Opens
events.blurb: The French-designed 193-kilometre sea-level canal linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea — dug largely by corvée (unpaid forced) Egyptian labour over ten years with massive loss of life — opened to international traffic. A procession of 68 ships led by a French imperial yacht sailed from Port Said to the Red Sea over four days. The canal cut the sea route from London to Bombay by about 7,200 kilometres and shifted the geography of global trade.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1869 — designer Ferdinand de Lesseps. Giuseppe Verdi's opera Aida, commissioned by Khedive Ismail for the opening, arrived too late and premiered in 1871. The canal was nationalized by Egypt in 1956, triggering the Suez Crisis.

events.title: Fall of France
