events.blurb: German armoured divisions crossed a forested highland deemed impassable by military doctrine, bypassed the most elaborate fixed defences in Europe, and in six weeks forced the capitulation of a nation whose army was considered the strongest on the continent. An armistice was signed in the same railway carriage used for the previous war's peace.
events.revealBlurb: May 10 – June 22, 1940. The armistice was signed at Compiègne in Hitler's deliberate reversal of the 1918 Armistice humiliation — he had the original railway carriage brought out of a museum. France lost 92,000 killed in six weeks. A junior general named de Gaulle flew to London and refused to accept the result.

events.title: Lend-Lease Act Signed
events.blurb: A nation officially at peace passed legislation allowing its president to lend, lease, or otherwise transfer war materials to any country whose defence he deemed vital to national security, bypassing a strict neutrality law without technically entering the conflict. The first shipments moved within weeks, directed at an island nation running critically short of everything.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1941 — FDR signed H.R. 1776 (the bill number was a deliberate wink). By the end of the programme, the US had shipped $50 billion in supplies — equivalent to roughly $800 billion today — to 38 countries. The Soviet Union received about 17 million tons of equipment, including 400,000 jeeps and trucks.

events.title: Operation Barbarossa
events.blurb: Three million soldiers, 600,000 motorised vehicles, 3,600 tanks, and 2,700 aircraft crossed a 2,900-kilometre border in the pre-dawn darkness, launching the largest land invasion in military history. The defender's air force lost over a thousand planes in the first day, many of them still on the ground.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1941. Stalin reportedly refused to believe his own border commanders' early reports and assumed the attacks were unauthorised provocations. The operation's codename referenced the medieval Holy Roman Emperor Frederick Barbarossa. By December, Germany had advanced 1,000 km but failed to knock the Soviet Union out of the war.

events.title: Death of Franklin Roosevelt
events.blurb: A president who had led his country through twelve years of depression and global conflict collapsed while sitting for a portrait at a cottage in the hills, dying two hours later before anyone could reach him, leaving a vice president who had been kept so far from the centre of power that he did not even know his government had been secretly building an atomic bomb.
events.revealBlurb: April 12, 1945 — FDR died at 3:35 PM at the Little White House in Warm Springs, Georgia. Harry Truman was presiding over the Senate when a note summoned him to the White House. His first question to Eleanor Roosevelt was whether he could do anything for her; she replied: "Is there anything we can do for you? For you are the one in trouble now."

events.title: Potsdam Conference
events.blurb: The three great powers met for the last time in an occupied defeated nation's suburbs, dividing it into occupation zones, setting reparations terms, and issuing an ultimatum to a remaining Asian adversary — while one leader discreetly mentioned to another that his country had recently successfully tested a weapon of extraordinary destructive power, which the other already knew about from spies.
events.revealBlurb: July 17 – August 2, 1945. Truman told Stalin the US had "a new weapon of unusual destructive force" — Trinity had been tested the previous day. Stalin showed no reaction; his spies had briefed him months earlier. Churchill lost the British general election mid-conference and was replaced by Clement Attlee, who turned up having learned the secrets only days before.

events.title: North American Video Game Crash
events.blurb: The home video game market had grown so fast that no one noticed it had filled up with garbage. Retailers were buried in unsold cartridges, consumers had lost all trust, and by 1985 an industry that had been worth $3.2 billion two years earlier had collapsed to $100 million — a 97 percent decline. Atari buried millions of unsold cartridges in a New Mexico landfill.
events.revealBlurb: 1983–1985 — Annual revenue fell from $3.2 billion (1983) to approximately $100 million (1985). The Atari landfill in Alamogordo, New Mexico — long an urban legend — was excavated in April 2014 and confirmed to contain millions of E.T. cartridges.

events.title: Sonic the Hedgehog Released for Sega Genesis
events.blurb: Sega needed a mascot to fight Mario. The result was a blue hedgehog who could run faster than the screen could scroll, built around a physics engine that turned speed itself into the core gameplay mechanic. It shipped bundled with the Genesis in North America, helped Sega capture 65 percent of the console market.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1991 — Sonic the Hedgehog launched in North America for the Sega Genesis. Sega's North American market share climbed from 15% to 65% during the game's first year. The Sonic franchise has since sold over 1.5 billion games.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: Pokémon GO Launches
events.blurb: A mobile game using GPS and augmented reality sent tens of millions of people into parks, cemeteries, and government buildings to catch fictional creatures on their phones. It broke multiple App Store records in its first 24 hours. Police stations issued public statements asking players not to enter. Central Park held impromptu gatherings of thousands at midnight.
events.revealBlurb: July 6, 2016 — Pokémon GO launched in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand. It surpassed 100 million downloads in under 30 days and generated $207 million in its first month — the highest ever for a mobile game. Lifetime revenue has surpassed $6 billion.

events.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Released
events.blurb: A cowboy open-world game with a 60-hour main story, simulated beard growth, morality consequences for every interaction, and a horse whose bond with the player affected its responsiveness opened the largest weekend in entertainment history. It earned $725 million in three days.
events.revealBlurb: October 26, 2018 — Red Dead Redemption 2 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. It shipped 17 million copies in its first thirteen days. The game has now sold over 79 million copies. Development reportedly involved teams working 100-hour weeks across five years.

events.title: Berlin Airlift Begins
events.blurb: When Soviet forces blockaded all land and water routes into the western sectors of a divided city, Western powers responded with the largest humanitarian airlift in history. At peak, a transport plane landed every 30 seconds, carrying 8,000 tons of coal, flour, and medicine a day to 2.5 million stranded residents.
events.revealBlurb: June 24, 1948 — the blockade began; the airlift launched two days later and ran 15 months. Pilots dropped candy bars on tiny parachutes for watching children; one became known as the "Candy Bomber." 101 people died during the operation.

events.title: Korean War Begins
events.blurb: In the pre-dawn darkness, roughly 75,000 soldiers of a northern peninsular state poured south across the 38th parallel, overwhelming border defenses and driving south within days. The United Nations Security Council, with the Soviet representative boycotting, voted to intervene — the first shooting war between major powers since 1945.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1950 — Kim Il-sung's forces crossed the parallel. The USSR was boycotting the UN over China's representation, which is why the Soviet veto didn't stop intervention. MacArthur's Inchon landing three months later turned the war.

events.title: Solidarity Founded
events.blurb: A strike at a shipyard in a Polish coastal city, led by an electrician who had been fired for union organizing, forced the communist government to sign an agreement permitting an independent, self-governing trade union — the first in the eastern bloc. Within a year ten million workers had joined. Martial law followed in December 1981, but the genie was out.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1980 — the Gdańsk Agreement. Electrician Lech Wałęsa would win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 and become Poland's first post-communist president in 1990. The movement's red logo, hand-painted in a shipyard, became an icon.

events.title: August Coup Against Gorbachev
events.blurb: A committee of Soviet hardliners — the KGB chief, the defense minister, the vice president — placed the reform-minded Soviet leader under house arrest at his Black Sea dacha and announced on state television that he was "unwell." Three days of confusion followed. A reformist Russian president climbed atop a tank outside his parliament and defied the plotters. The coup collapsed in 60 hours, and so, effectively, did the union.
events.revealBlurb: August 19-21, 1991 — the tank-top defier was Boris Yeltsin. Gorbachev returned to Moscow to find his authority gutted; Yeltsin had eclipsed him. Within four months the USSR itself would be gone.

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: Prince's Purple Rain Released
events.blurb: A 26-year-old Minneapolis musician released his sixth studio album — the soundtrack to a semi-autobiographical feature film he had also starred in. The album's nine tracks combined funk, rock, R&B, and gospel into a sound that critics had long despaired of finding. It sat at number one on the Billboard 200 for 24 consecutive weeks. The artist held a complex, rivalrous relationship with Michael Jackson's Thriller era.
events.revealBlurb: June 25, 1984 — Prince and the Revolution. The accompanying film grossed $68 million on a $7 million budget. The album's singles "When Doves Cry" and "Let's Go Crazy" both hit #1. Prince died in 2016 at 57 from an accidental fentanyl overdose.

events.title: We Are the World Recorded
events.blurb: Forty-five American pop stars gathered at a Los Angeles recording studio after the annual American Music Awards ceremony to record a charity single for African famine relief, written by two headliners in a single evening. The recording session ran until 8 AM. The single sold over 20 million copies and raised more than $63 million. Its producer had hung a sign at the studio entrance reading: "Check your ego at the door."
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1985 — written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie; produced by Quincy Jones. Participating artists included Stevie Wonder, Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan, Diana Ross, and Ray Charles. The sign was Jones's idea. A 2024 Netflix documentary rehashed the making of the track.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Hands Across America
events.blurb: Around 6.5 million Americans paid $10 each to stand along a 6,754-kilometre line stretching from a California beach to a New York skyscraper, holding hands for fifteen minutes as part of a charity event to raise money for hunger and homelessness relief. The line required one person every 0.77 metres; roughly half the route was inhabited uninterrupted, the rest had gaps. The event raised $34 million after expenses and was widely considered more spectacle than effective philanthropy.
events.revealBlurb: May 25, 1986 — organized by USA for Africa. The line ran from the Santa Monica Pier to the Battery in Manhattan via 16 states and DC. A theme song was recorded by over 500 celebrities. The event inspired the 2019 horror film "Us," where the hand-holding line takes on sinister significance.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: Intel 4004 Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the first commercial microprocessor — a single integrated circuit 3 millimetres long containing 2,300 transistors, clocking at 740 kilohertz, capable of computing roughly as fast as the 30-tonne ENIAC 25 years earlier. It had been developed as a calculator chip for a Japanese customer. Its designers convinced Intel's management to retain the design rights and market it as a general-purpose product.
events.revealBlurb: November 15, 1971 — Intel 4004. Designers Federico Faggin, Ted Hoff, Stanley Mazor, and Masatoshi Shima. The 4-bit chip cost $200. Intel's 1971 product-line predecessor was the 3101 memory chip; it now sells trillions of transistors per year.

events.title: Apple Computer Founded
events.blurb: Two 20-something Californians, a college dropout and a self-taught engineer, formed a partnership to sell a printed-circuit-board computer design the engineer had developed and the dropout had realized was marketable. A third partner, older and more cautious, asked out within two weeks and sold his share back for $800. The initial product was a hand-built board requiring the buyer to supply their own power supply, keyboard, and case.
events.revealBlurb: April 1, 1976 — Steve Jobs, Steve Wozniak, and Ronald Wayne. Wayne's 10 percent share would today be worth over $300 billion. He has said he doesn't regret selling out; he'd been in a startup before and wanted to avoid another personal-liability exposure.

events.title: Sony Walkman Released
events.blurb: A Japanese electronics company released a portable personal cassette player, weighing 390 grams, with headphones instead of a speaker. It had no record function — unusual for a cassette player — and its CEO personally insisted on this as a way of encouraging private, solitary music consumption. The device created an entirely new product category and pulled portable listening out of the car radio and boombox and into the individual's pocket for the next quarter-century.
events.revealBlurb: July 1, 1979 — Sony TPS-L2. Co-founder Masaru Ibuka had wanted something compact to enjoy opera on long flights. The original name in Japan was "Walkman"; in the US, "Soundabout"; in the UK, "Stowaway." "Walkman" eventually won out globally.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: Tesla Model S Released
events.blurb: A California electric-vehicle startup, founded a decade earlier and funded partly by the same entrepreneur who had sold PayPal, delivered the first units of a four-door luxury sedan with a fully electric drivetrain, over-the-air software updates, a 17-inch touchscreen, and a 500-kilometre range. Legacy automakers had considered electric cars a niche; the Model S made them convincingly better than gasoline vehicles in several important dimensions.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 2012 — Tesla Model S, led by Elon Musk. Motor Trend named it Car of the Year. The "Ludicrous Mode" software option made it accelerate 0-60 mph in under 3 seconds. Tesla passed $1 trillion valuation in 2021, briefly the first automaker to do so.

events.title: Hotmail Launched
events.blurb: Two engineers launched the world's first free web-based email service, deliberately choosing the launch date to coincide with a major American holiday celebrating independence. Users for the first time could access their email from any computer with a browser, independent of any particular ISP or employer. The service picked up a million users in six months.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1996 — Sabeer Bhatia and Jack Smith. They chose Independence Day to symbolize freedom from ISP lock-in. Microsoft acquired the service for $400 million 18 months later; it evolved into Outlook.com.

events.title: Wikipedia Launched
events.blurb: A 34-year-old internet entrepreneur who had been trying to build an online encyclopedia by paying credentialed experts to write and peer-review articles gave up on the slow model and switched to a radical alternative: a wiki, editable by anyone. The new version grew faster than expected. It had more articles in its first year than the slow-model version had produced in a previous eighteen months.
events.revealBlurb: January 15, 2001 — Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. By 2007 Wikipedia had surpassed Britannica in size and approximately in accuracy. Today's English Wikipedia has over 6.9 million articles, and the full project runs in 340+ languages.

events.title: iTunes Store Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched an online music store selling individual songs for 99 cents each, a pricing decision its CEO had to personally negotiate with record-label executives deeply suspicious of any further internet disruption. The store sold a million downloads in its first six days. Within four years, it was the largest music retailer in the United States.
events.revealBlurb: April 28, 2003 — Apple. Steve Jobs had threaten to "pull the plug" on the negotiations at one point. The catalogue launched with 200,000 songs, Mac-only; Windows compatibility came in October. The per-song price model reshaped the music industry.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Reddit Founded
events.blurb: Two 22-year-old University of Virginia roommates who had just moved to Massachusetts on a Y Combinator fellowship launched a link-aggregation and discussion site that would, over the next two decades, become what its users called "the front page of the internet." The initial userbase was boosted by the founders themselves maintaining dozens of fake accounts to seed discussions. They sold the site to Condé Nast 16 months later for a reported $10-20 million.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 2005 — Steve Huffman and Alexis Ohanian; later joined by Aaron Swartz, the open-internet activist who would die in 2013 facing federal prosecution. The site's iconic mascot, Snoo, was designed by Ohanian on a napkin.

events.title: NAACP Founded
events.blurb: A biracial group of activists, scholars, and newspaper editors met at a New York conference on the centennial of Abraham Lincoln's birth to establish an organization dedicated to fighting racial discrimination through legal action and public advocacy. W.E.B. Du Bois, the Harvard-trained sociologist, edited its magazine The Crisis; its lawyers would eventually argue Brown v. Board of Education.
events.revealBlurb: February 12, 1909 — National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. It was founded partly in response to the Springfield, Illinois race riot the year before. Du Bois served as editor of The Crisis for 24 years.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court unanimously ruled that racially segregated public schools are "inherently unequal" and therefore unconstitutional, overturning the 58-year-old "separate but equal" doctrine. The narrow ruling on schools would expand over the next decade to strike down segregation in parks, beaches, swimming pools, and every other public facility.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Chief Justice Earl Warren assembled a 9-0 majority despite internal resistance. Enforcement took years; Arkansas governors called out the national guard to bar Black students, and some counties closed their schools entirely rather than integrate.

events.title: Freedom Riders Depart
events.blurb: Thirteen volunteers — seven Black, six white — boarded buses in Washington, D.C. bound for New Orleans to test a recent Supreme Court ruling outlawing segregated interstate travel facilities. In Alabama their bus was firebombed outside Anniston and the riders beaten bloody by a mob in Birmingham. They kept riding. Subsequent waves continued through the summer.
events.revealBlurb: May 4, 1961 — sponsored by CORE. A 21-year-old John Lewis was among them and had his skull fractured. Attorney General Robert Kennedy called for a "cooling-off period;" CORE leader James Farmer replied: "We've been cooling off for 100 years."

events.title: Civil Rights Act of 1964 Signed
events.blurb: President Lyndon Johnson signed the most sweeping civil rights legislation since Reconstruction, outlawing discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, or national origin in employment and public accommodations — ending the legal architecture of Jim Crow segregation. The bill passed after the longest Senate filibuster in history: 57 days.
events.revealBlurb: July 2, 1964 — The White House. Johnson reportedly told an aide after signing the bill, "We have lost the South for a generation" — a reference to the political realignment he expected. Johnson signed the bill with 75 ceremonial pens, handing them to civil rights leaders and the bill's sponsors.

events.title: Stonewall Riots
events.blurb: A routine police raid on a Mafia-owned gay bar in a Greenwich Village of Manhattan turned into a six-night uprising when patrons — many of them drag queens, street kids, and trans people of color — fought back rather than submit to arrest. The confrontation catalyzed the modern LGBTQ rights movement; the first Pride marches were held on its first anniversary.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 1969 — Stonewall Inn, NYC. Pivotal figures included Marsha P. Johnson and Sylvia Rivera. The riot ignited the Gay Liberation Front, which modeled itself on the Black Panthers. June is now Pride Month across much of the world.

events.title: Babe Ruth Sold to Yankees
events.blurb: A Boston baseball team's owner, needing cash to finance a Broadway musical he had invested in, sold the star pitcher and outfielder of his defending World Series champion team to the rival New York franchise for $100,000 cash plus a $300,000 loan secured by the team's stadium. The deal shipped the best player in baseball to the Yankees; Boston did not win another World Series for 86 years. Yankee championships followed in a cascade.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 1920 — Red Sox owner Harry Frazee sold Ruth to the Yankees. The musical was "No, No, Nanette" (1925); its eventual success does not redeem the sale. Ruth would hit 714 career home runs, lead the Yankees to 7 pennants, and define American sport for a generation.

events.title: Pelé Wins First World Cup
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Brazilian forward, playing in his first senior international tournament, scored two goals in the World Cup final as Brazil beat the host nation 5-2 to win football's greatest prize for the first time in the country's history. He became the youngest player ever to score in a World Cup final; his performance vaulted Brazilian football onto the world stage. He would go on to win two more World Cups over the following 12 years.
events.revealBlurb: June 29, 1958 — Pelé (Edson Arantes do Nascimento) at the Råsunda Stadium, Solna, Sweden. Brazil 5, Sweden 2. Pelé was carried off the field by his teammates at the end. He remains the only player to win three World Cups.

events.title: Wilt Chamberlain's 100-Point Game
events.blurb: A 25-year-old 7-foot-1 Philadelphia Warriors center scored 100 points in a regular-season NBA game — 36 field goals, 28 free throws, a record that has never been approached since. The game, played at a neutral-site arena in a central Pennsylvania city, drew only 4,124 spectators; no television footage survives, and only one photograph of the 100-point moment exists. The center himself had scored 50 on a different occasion just weeks earlier; a 100-point game almost seemed inevitable.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1962 — Wilt Chamberlain, Philadelphia vs. New York Knicks at Hershey, PA. Final score: Warriors 169, Knicks 147. The iconic photo shows Chamberlain holding a piece of paper reading "100" in the locker room. His career scoring average of 30.1 points per game remains second only to Michael Jordan.

events.title: Maradona's Hand of God & Goal of the Century
events.blurb: An Argentine forward, playing a World Cup quarterfinal against England four years after a war over Atlantic islands the two countries had fought, scored two goals in four minutes. The first was a blatant handball that the referee missed; the player later described it as scored "a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God." The second, four minutes later, was a solo 60-metre dribble past five English players from the halfway line — widely considered the greatest goal in World Cup history.
events.revealBlurb: June 22, 1986 — Diego Maradona at Estadio Azteca, Mexico City. Argentina 2, England 1. Argentina went on to win the tournament. Maradona later admitted the first goal was not only illegal but intended as a kind of revenge for the Falklands War. He died at 60 in 2020; Argentina went into three days of national mourning.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Tunguska Event
events.blurb: A massive explosion in the atmosphere above a remote Siberian forest flattened some 80 million trees over an area of 2,150 square kilometres. Eyewitnesses 60 kilometres away were thrown from their chairs. Seismic stations across Europe registered the blast. The first scientific expedition did not reach the site for 19 years. No impact crater was ever found.
events.revealBlurb: June 30, 1908 — Tunguska, Russian Empire. Current consensus: a stony asteroid 50-60 metres across exploded about 8 kilometres up. If it had arrived five hours later, it would have hit St. Petersburg. The date is now International Asteroid Day.

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Typhoon Haiyan
events.blurb: One of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall — with sustained winds of 315 km/h — struck the central Philippines, obliterating coastal cities. A 7-metre storm surge drove ships onto city streets; the city of Tacloban lost most of its infrastructure. At least 6,300 people died, and 4 million were displaced.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2013 — Leyte province. The Filipino lead negotiator at the UN climate talks that week gave a tearful speech and began a hunger strike until "meaningful progress" was made. His country's delegation wore black.
